extracted.intended_audience: architects and builders of middle-class dwelling houses (designers, sanitary authorities, building contractors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical sanitary and construction guidance for designing and building healthy, comfortable middle-class houses, covering site selection, foundations, walls, roofs, heating, ventilation, drainage, refuse disposal, and sanitary fittings. Emphasizes materials, detailing, and oversight to avoid damp, sewer-gas, and decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site selection and localities
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the localities in which dwellings are to be situated; certain localities are more generally healthy than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where occupants must live in less healthy districts, attempt improvement by planting, subdrainage, and similar measures. The architect should take locality into account when planning to secure a sweet home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil and subsoil protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not leave top soil inclosed within the walls of houses; subsoil may need covering with a layer of cement concrete and sometimes asphalt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subsoil is damp moisture will rise; if porous, offensive matter may percolate. Much cold dampness is caused by moisture rising from ground inclosed within outer walls; protect subsoil under floors with damp-proof layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellar construction and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Cellars should be constructed with damp-proof walls and floors; admit light freely; ventilate every part; avoid taking in any drain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If cellars are unnecessary they are often harmful; where used ensure water cannot pass through walls/floors so no drain is required. Light and air must not be shut out; cellars are a favorite means of entrance for sickness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damp course over whole walls
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a good damp course over the whole of the walls, internal as well as external.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damp course is essential; do not omit for internal walls. Materials: glazed earthenware perforated slabs (best if cost allows), slates bedded in cement above and below, asphalt where ground irregular. Avoid gas tar and sand (deteriorates). Place damp course above ground level and below ground floor joists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basement wall protection
rubrics_metrics.description: If a basement story exists, outer walls below ground should be built hollow or coated externally with a substance impervious to wet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hollow construction or external coating prevents penetration; combine with a proper damp course to protect basement space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of external wall materials and jointing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use materials for outer walls that are as impervious to wet as possible; jointing should be non-absorbent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid very porous materials which absorb water and on drying cause cold by evaporation. If brick/stone are non-porous but mortar is porous, water will be sucked in at joints. Select low-porosity brick/stone and matching durable mortar/jointing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cavity/hollow or lined walls
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-built hollow walls or stone walls lined with brick and a cavity between are recommended to keep houses dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave a cavity (e.g., half-inch cavity filled with waterproofing composition) between outer and inner portions; fill/run with appropriate waterproof composition as building rises; cavities improve waterproofing and strengthen walls and can serve as a damp course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hygeian Rock Building Composition (waterproofing material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider new waterproofing materials (e.g., Hygeian Rock Building Composition) correctly applied to make walls waterproof and strengthen them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When properly applied it can be of great utility; may also be used as a damp course. Architect must test and determine suitability under circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roof waterproofing and heat-tightness
rubrics_metrics.description: Roofs must be watertight, weathertight, and also 'heat-tight' to retain warmth in cold weather and exclude heat in hot weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under tiles and particularly under slates provide non-conducting substance (boarding, felt, or pugging). Ensure suitable pitch to prevent entry of rain or snow in windy weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roof boarding and gutter/flat detailing
rubrics_metrics.description: Boarding under gutters/flats should be laid in narrow widths and in the direction of fall to avoid cockling which forms ridges/ furrows where water rests and decays metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly laid boarding causes water to stand and decay gutters/metal; pay great care to laying boarding correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eaves spouting and rain-water downpipe sizing and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Eaves spouting should be of ample size; rain-water down pipes should be at frequent intervals and of suitable diameter; outlets should not be contracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover outlets with wire gratings to prevent leaf-choking. Ensure watertight joints to avoid sewer gas escape where connected with soil drains. Provide siphon trap at bottom of each downpipe unless used as a ventilator to the drains (then ensure perfect jointing and that outlet is above windows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance and painting of guttering and downpipes
rubrics_metrics.description: Eaves spouting and downpipes should be periodically examined and cleaned out; paint inside and out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not painted iron will rust and flake off, causing stoppages; periodic inspection prevents decay and stops sewer gas ingress via faulty joints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid continual dampness (prevent decay and odors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continual dampness causes chemical action and decay of building materials (wood, wallpapers, paste, size, plaster), producing injurious exhalations and bad smells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select good quality materials (avoid quickly grown sappy timber, sour paste, stale size, wall papers with injurious pigments). Use sea-sand or salt-containing sand neither for plaster nor mortar. Prevent humid atmosphere via ventilation and dry construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful selection of plaster and mortar materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials for plaster and mortar must be free from organic matter and salts to prevent formation of nitrates/deliquescent salts which attract moisture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sea sand or salt-containing sand should never be used. Poor materials result in blistering, peeling, detachment of wallpaper, and deterioration under humid conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architect's responsibility and on-site supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: The architect must test materials/apparatus, ensure their proper application, and supervise workmen so sanitary details are carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architects must not blindly follow precedent; they must exercise insight into natural laws and employ serviceable appliances, and ensure workmen are trustworthy. Many defects arise where instructions or details are covered up and poorly executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heating system evaluation (open fires vs alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open fireplaces are wasteful, dirty, and often injurious to health; alternatives (ventilating grates, closed stoves, slow-combustion stoves, steam/hot water systems) have advantages and require careful design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ventilating grates admit external air to back of grate to reduce cold draughts — beneficial if free from smoke ingress. Closed stoves are more economical but risk charging air with combustion products; slow-combustion stoves avoid that. Centralized steam heating can be useful (can locate furnace away and heat multiple dwellings) but requires special and adequate ventilation. Gas stoves can be expensive and difficult to prevent combustion products entering the dwelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: A constant change of air in every part of dwellings is absolutely necessary for a sweet home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open fireplaces help ventilation but can draw impure air from other parts if the house is otherwise unsanitary. Central heating systems must include adequate ventilation provisions to avoid accumulation of organic combustion particles and carbonic acid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighting and gas safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial lighting (candle, oil, gas) contaminates room atmosphere; gas in particular can be injurious and leaks impregnate soil with poisonous matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hopes for electric lighting to obviate combustion contamination. Gas pipes should be laid where easily examined and repaired (in France exposed by law except where unavoidable). Embedded pipes are hard to inspect and repair; leakages are common and taint air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitchen design and fume removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooking ranges should be constructed to carry off fumes; kitchens must be well ventilated and so placed that fumes cannot enter other parts of the dwelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooking odors may condense on surfaces and later putrefy; washing-day steam should be isolated or ventilated by placing washhouse disconnected from living parts or providing well-constructed boiler/furnace and flue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse disposal and ash receptacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use open ash-pits close to the house where organic refuse can rot; replace with small galvanized iron covered receptacles on wheels to be emptied every two or three days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where gardens exist, refuse is useful as manure and should be stored far from dwellings. Otherwise burn refuse promptly (in a close range or open fire with care) rather than letting it rot in pits which are pest-boxes causing sickness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privy/cesspool siting and design
rubrics_metrics.description: Privies may be tolerated in the country when distant from houses, but in crowded neighborhoods are abominations; cesspools should be avoided, ventilated, watertight, and never near dwellings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cesspools can percolate foul matter and contaminate water supply. Earth closets if carefully attended and emptied can be used indoors, but in towns disposal is difficult. Avoid placing rain-water tanks under dwellings that might be contaminated by sewage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water closet (W.C.) construction and pan design
rubrics_metrics.description: Use properly constructed water-closet apparatus; banish pan closets and avoid funnel-shaped W.C. pans which retain dirt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: W.C. pan should be large and retain a layer of water at the bottom, to be swept out by the rush of service water. Outlet may be side-connected to an earthenware S-trap with ventilating outlet through the wall. Funnel-shaped pans are objectionable because they catch and retain dirt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil pipe, traps, and venting for water closets
rubrics_metrics.description: Soil pipe should be a strong 4 in. iron pipe, carefully jointed and watertight, continued of the same size to above the tops of all windows; its foot should connect to a ventilating trap to cut off air connection between house and drains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer taking soil pipe immediately through wall from S-trap then connect to iron pipe. Ensure watertight jointing and continuation above windows to prevent sewer-gas ingress. Disconnecting and ventilating traps are vital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation/disconnection for wastes (baths, sinks, urinals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wastes from baths, sinks, and urinals should be ventilated and disconnected from drains or discharged above a gulley trap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disconnect or ventilate to prevent foul air/backflow; ensure discharge arrangements avoid direct connection that could allow sewer gas into rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and laying of house drains (materials & workmanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use glazed stoneware pipe for house drains (well-burnt, well-glazed, free from twist); lay trenches to proper falls; where ground is soft lay pipes on concrete; joint with cement or well-tempered clay and wipe away projecting portions inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear passage-way is essential. Badly joined/irregularly laid pipes cause accumulation, fermentation and sewer-gas. Too much care cannot be exercised in laying pipes properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer straight-line drains with man-holes/lamp-holes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid curved angles in drains; lay them in straight lines from point to point and insert man-holes or lamp-holes at every angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straight runs with man-holes ease inspection and clearance. Man-holes/lamp-holes may also be used for ventilating and flushing the drains; Local Government Board insists on this for public buildings and it is advisable for house-drains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of disconnecting trap before main sewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Each house drain should have a disconnecting trap just before it enters the main sewer to cut off air connection between house-drains and the main sewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects occupants from sewer-gas developed elsewhere. Without it poison may be conveyed from external defects to the house. Disconnecting trap is a critical sanitary detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of inspection and maintenance of drains
rubrics_metrics.description: Design drains so that the whole system can be easily examined and stoppages quickly removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because opening drains is costly, defects may go unrepaired until illness occurs. Straight runs and man-holes make inspection practical; man-holes can be used for ventilation and flushing to maintain cleanliness.
